Think about the last time someone asked you to trust them with something important

you probably wanted a little more than just their word, right?

now imagine that the person making decisions is not human. Its an AI agent and the decision could affect real money sitting in a smart contract.

the contract gets an answer but how does it know the work behind that answer was done correctly?

That is the part worth thinking about.

<trust is easy to claim>

this is what caught my attention about @BaranosAI 

baranos uses deterministic LLM inference and an onchain challenge process to make AI computation verifiable.

an executor submits a result along with commitments to its computation.. watchers can independently recompute the output and challenge dishonest work..if the challenge succeeds, the dishonest party can lose its bond.

instead of asking everyone to simply trust the provider, there is a way to check its work.

where I'd take this on Fogo??

imagine a lending protocol trying to assess risk.

an AI agent reviews available borrower information and recommends a risk category. That recommendation could influence how the protocol handles a loan so blindly accepting the answer would be a bad idea.

I'd explore using baranos to verify the AI computation before the protocol considers its result, with the smart contract enforcing clear lending rules on fogo.

Its a proposed use case not something I'm claiming already exists and fogo's fast blocks are interesting here but speed isn't the whole story. 

barano's current documentation says some workloads can take minutes to hours to complete and settle.

there's still a catch!!

even if the computation checks out the AI can still make a poor recommendation because its data is incomplete or its model is flawed.

verification doesn't make AI infallible. It helps answer a narrower question.. was the agreed computation carried out correctly?

that distinction matters when real assets are involved.

as AI agents take on more work onchain.. I think we'll need more than answers that sound convincing.

We'll need ways to check the work behind them.

that's the potential I see in @BaranosAI and why I'd like to explore what's possible on @fogo

text:
Putting IP onchain is only half the story

The bigger challenge is making sure people and AI agents know what they are actually allowed to do with it.

Imagine an AI agent finding a song for a video. It can identify the track, but can it use it commercially? Is remixing allowed? Has the required licence been obtained?

Today, these details are often stored in contracts or platform databases, making them difficult to check automatically.

This is where ERC-8432 gets interesting

On October 6, @soneium  announced its intention to support ERC-8432, an open standard for an Onchain IP Asset and License Registry.

The goal is to give applications and AI agents a common way to:

→ Identify IP assets across registries and chains
→ Read machine-readable licence terms
→ Record and verify licence agreements onchain
→ Check permissions programmatically before using an asset

One technical detail I find interesting is how each record is identified using (chainId, registry, id). This helps applications locate the correct asset or agreement without depending on one central registry.
The standard also supports independent registries and can work with ERC-721 IP tokens. Its validation hooks are designed to support dynamic permission checks.
It can also connect with other emerging tools, such as ERC-8004 for AI agent identity and x402 for payments, without making them mandatory dependencies.

Think about the workflow: a creator registers a recording and publishes its licence terms. An AI agent discovers the track, checks whether its intended use is allowed, and obtains the required agreement. The application can then verify that agreement onchain before using the track.

This could make licensing easier to integrate across compliant apps, marketplaces and AI agents, without requiring a separate integration for every platform.

But one thing is important: ERC-8432 standardises how licensing information and agreements are represented and checked. It does not automatically define legal rights or make every use permissible.

@soneium  is inviting builders to review the draft and help shape the standard. It is still a proposed standard, so the real impact will depend on implementation and adoption.

For me, this is an important step towards making onchain IP more useful.

Ownership tells us who holds an asset. Licensing helps establish what others are allowed to do with it.

As AI-generated content grows, making those permissions readable and verifiable could become increasingly important

text:
Stop overcomplicating AI agents.

An agent is a loop:

1. Give the model a task and a list of tools
2. The model picks a tool
3. Your code runs it and sends the result back
4. Repeat until the model has an answer

Underneath the layers, agent frameworks follow that same basic loop. 

Yet teams spend months comparing them before shipping a single agent. 

Write the loop yourself with plain API calls, and a lot of the confusion clears up.

This summer, we built one for a PE-backed healthcare billing company. Whenever a client questioned a revenue report, an expert had to write SQL by hand against a legacy schema to find the answer. 

Now they can ask those questions in plain English, and the agent finds the answers in their claims data.

Building the loop was straightforward. The actual work was in the evals: checking the agent’s answers against verified results from their claims data.

We built the answer key alongside the agent from day one. Their team gave us real questions and the SQL they’d write to answer them. We started with 10 questions, ran the full set every cycle, and kept adding more. By the first deployment, we had 60. 

The agent answered 59 correctly. Its answer to the key question, “Which denials were preventable?”, reconciles to the penny with the database.

Six weeks in, their CPTO was testing it with real questions. When they challenged one answer, the agent acknowledged the mistake and corrected it.

That’s what you need to get right: the loop, a check on every output, and a set of real questions you run again after every change. RAG, MCP, and multi-agent setups come in when you have a specific problem for them to solve.

So pick one question your business still answers by hand. Build the loop with one tool. Put together 10 questions with answers your people trust, and keep improving the agent until it gets them right.

You’ll learn more in two weeks than in months of testing agent frameworks.

A 3D reconstruction can be verified and still fail to deliver what the buyer actually needs.

That’s an important part of the workflow I’ve been thinking about with @vangrid_io .

An AI agent can request a location, fund a bounty in USDC, and receive a reconstructed 3D scene after a contributor captures the place. Privacy protection and provenance records add another layer of trust, helping buyers check where the data came from.

But there’s another side to data quality: was the capture done for the right purpose?

If a robotics team needs a clear view of a warehouse aisle, or a logistics company needs details about a loading entrance, the request must explain exactly what matters. Otherwise, even a valid, verified capture may miss the details needed for the job.

That’s why the bounty brief matters so much. Clear requirements around angles, coverage, and important features can make the difference between an impressive mesh and useful spatial data.

For Vangrid, reliable provenance builds trust in the capture, while precise requests help make the result valuable.

The goal isn’t just to capture the real world. It’s to capture the right information for the people who need it.

text:
AI agents from @termix_ai from tools that only generate outputs into participants that can actually interact with an economic marketplace. Instead of an agent simply telling a user how to complete a task, it can discover available work, make offers, fund an order, provide a service, and handle delivery. That creates a more complete workflow where the agent can move from understanding a task to taking action. 

The connection with coding agents makes this especially interesting because developers can work with marketplace services without building a separate integration for every agent. It creates a common path for different agents to interact with the same marketplace.

Another important concept is interoperability between agents and services. If every AI agent requires its own custom connection, scaling an agent economy becomes difficult because every new participant adds more integration work. 

A shared framework can reduce that friction by giving different agents a common way to discover and interact with available services. This means the marketplace can potentially grow without requiring every agent to be rebuilt from scratch. The more standardized that interaction becomes, the easier it could be for different agents to work together. That is an important foundation for a larger agent economy.

The bigger shift is that agents become capable of making decisions and executing multiple steps within a workflow. 

An agent in @termix_ai could identify a task, find an appropriate service, submit an offer, handle the transaction, and receive the completed result. That makes the agent less like a chatbot and more like an autonomous worker operating within defined rules. 

It also creates new questions around permissions, verification, accountability, and spending limits. As agents gain more ability to act independently, those supporting systems become increasingly important.

What makes this concept interesting is the possibility of agents becoming economic participants rather than simply software assistants. A marketplace could eventually have agents searching for opportunities, collaborating with other agents, purchasing specialized services, and completing jobs with limited human intervention. 

The important milestone would not simply be having more agents connected to the marketplace. It would be seeing agents repeatedly discover useful work, transact successfully, and complete real tasks from beginning to end. That is where the idea starts moving from AI automation toward an actual agent driven economy.

text:
A security researcher just bought the keys to Xiaomi, Huawei, NIO, and 7 government agencies. They were sitting in 6 terabytes of AI chat logs, for sale to anyone. The engineers at those companies leaked everything themselves and never noticed.

Here's how it works. China blocks direct access to Claude and ChatGPT, so engineers there buy access through middlemen, sketchy resellers on Taobao who pipe your requests to the real model for cheap. It feels exactly like using the real thing. Except the middleman reads every word you send.

And when you're using an AI coding tool, you send a lot. These agents upload your whole project so the model can help you. Config files, VPN setups, Aliyun cloud keys, GitLab logins for Xiaomi's internal servers and a national research lab. All of it flows through the reseller in plain text. He logs it. Then he sells the logs.

That's the dataset this researcher bought.

Spy agencies spend years and billions trying to get inside networks like these. Salt Typhoon burrowed into US telecoms forever just to intercept traffic. This pile assembled itself. Thousands of engineers asking an AI to fix their code, each one quietly shipping their employer's secrets to a stranger, one request at a time.

The team behind this (UCSB plus Fuzzland) already caught 26 of these resellers injecting malicious commands into AI responses, and says one drained $500K from a client's wallet. Honestly, the quiet logging scares me more. A reseller doesn't have to do anything evil to end up holding your keys. Reading the traffic is literally the job.

And before anyone in America feels smug, every company here is wiring coding agents into their stack right now through middleware nobody has vetted. The Chinese logs just went up for sale first.

text:
Linus didn't have Google, GitHub, Stack Overflow, AI coding agents.

But he wasn't building from zero, either.

In 1991, he had:
→ An Intel 80386 DX-33 PC with 4 MB RAM and a 40 MB hard drive. He bought it on January 5, 1991, for roughly 18,000 Finnish markka, paid in installments.

→ MINIX, Andrew Tanenbaum's educational Unix-like OS, which served as his development environment for months.

→ GCC to compile his C code.

→ Technical books and SunOS documentation to understand Unix.

→ Usenet to ask questions, get feedback, and eventually announce Linux to the world.

→ GNU tools like Bash to help turn his kernel into a useful system.

Here's a fun detail: he started by writing a tiny task-switcher that alternated between printing "AAAA" and "BBBB" on the screen to understand the 386.

No AI coding agents. No instant answers. Just curiosity, fundamentals, and a willingness to build.

His original announcement even described it as "just a hobby."

Linux started as a hobby. The rest is history.

text:
Your Mac shouldn’t stay awake all night just because an agent is running.

Adrafinil is a macOS menu bar app for builders who run AI coding agents.

It helps you keep a closed-lid Mac awake only while agent work is active by acquiring a sleep assertion at the start of work and releasing it when the work ends.

Key features:

• Agent-aware sleep control – normal sleep resumes when no agent session holds an assertion
• Nine agent hooks – an installer connects Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Aider, Hermes, OpenCode, Cline, and Pi
• Agent-driven holds – the bundled MCP tool or CLI can keep the Mac awake for a long build or deploy
• Overlapping session handling – reference-counted assertions release sleep only after the last session finishes
• Thermal and idle safeguards – assertions can be force-released on temperature thresholds or after an owning process is idle

It’s open-source (MIT license).

author: DanKornas

text:
Qwen3.8-27B just got a significant inference speed upgrade for NVIDIA GPU users with 16GB of VRAM or more.

A new contribution from niklaslenz_ai updates ExLlamaV3 to version 1.6.0 and replaces the model’s MTP head with a DFlash2 draft model.

The reported RTX 5090 results show substantial improvements across three workloads:

Prose generation
103 → 113 tokens/sec

Code generation
180 → 275 tokens/sec

Structured output
206 → 366 tokens/sec

That’s roughly 10% faster for prose, 53% for code, and 78% for structured generation.

The biggest gains appear in code and structured workloads, where decoding speed can make a noticeable difference when running local coding agents, generating JSON, or processing repetitive structured outputs.

The technical change is worth paying attention to. Speculative decoding uses a smaller or specialized draft model to propose tokens, while the main model verifies them. When enough proposed tokens are accepted, the system can generate more output per verification step.

DFlash2 provides a different drafting approach from the previous MTP setup, and these results suggest that pairing it with the updated ExLlamaV3 runtime can improve throughput considerably on the tested RTX 5090 configuration.

Other GPUs could benefit too. RTX 3090, RTX 4090, and RTX 5070 Ti owners are encouraged to test the updated setup, but comparable benchmark numbers have not yet been confirmed for those cards.

Keep in mind that results will depend on the GPU, quantization, workload, context length, and inference settings. The RTX 5090 figures shouldn’t be assumed to transfer directly to every setup.

If you’re already running Qwen3.8-27B locally, this update is worth investigating. Test your existing configuration against the new one and share the results so the community can build a clearer picture of the gains across different GPUs.

Running multiple coding agents shouldn’t make you their copy-paste relay.

Agent Room is an open-source MCP-based collaboration layer for developers coordinating coding agents across editors, vendors, and machines.

It helps you keep an agent team aligned by putting sessions in a shared room with structured decisions, tasks, and results instead of passing context between separate windows.

Key features:

• Shared rooms – agents join with a short room code from MCP clients or the web
• Structured artifacts – DECISION, TODO, STATUS, and RESULT markers turn chat into extractable work products
• Evidence-gated task board – tasks are submitted with evidence and verified by a different agent before completion
• Presence and turn modes – visible presence plus open, sequential, and moderator modes help coordinate the conversation
• Exportable reports – room_minutes can export a room into a shareable record such as minutes, an ADR, or a PR description

It’s open-source (MIT license).

text:
Benefits of the CAFE stack (@Cloudflare + @alchemy_run + @foldkit + @EffectTS_) for building software with coding agents:

1. Agents invent less architecture. They focus on product-level execution within a well-defined architecture. You build faster, with more confidence. You focus on what makes your product unique.

2. Your codebase becomes semantically rich. Intent and meaning are explicit rather than left for future agents to infer. Each new agent spends fewer tokens reconstructing intent.

3. Tests read like executable behavioral specs. Expected behavior is easy to inspect, and both humans and agents can verify implementations against it.

4. Strong conventions result in remarkably legible AI-generated code. Agents do what you expect more often, with less steering. The codebase feels consistent and predictable.

5. Explicitness makes behavior clear. Unexpected magic has fewer places to hide. Diffs are easier to review. Yes, it’s more LoC, but who cares when you’re not writing it by hand?

🧮 The billing mechanism for any request can be written as:
➤ Cost = (input tokens × input price + output tokens × output price) × (1 − discount).
➤ Input and output tokens are usually priced differently, so long prompts with short answers cost differently from short prompts with long answers.
➤ Metering records each component per request, which is what appears in usage logs.

🔍 This is why unified metering matters for cost control. When a developer switches from one model to another, the formula stays the same; only the prices and discount change. A single dashboard showing token counts across models makes those comparisons direct.

text:
For a while now, I've been trying to get people to look at Injective differently.

Not just as the chain for perps and DeFi, but as a network building financial infrastructure at the protocol level. And honestly, sometimes I feel like that part gets lost in the usual conversations about $INJ.

Then I came across CoinMarketCap's latest breakdown of @injective , and I was glad to see someone go deep into the architecture behind it.

Think about what it takes to build a trading application on a typical chain. You need market infrastructure, order matching, risk controls and settlement logic. Teams often have to build or integrate much of that themselves.

Injective takes a different approach. Its onchain order book and other financial primitives give applications shared infrastructure to build on, rather than forcing every project to start from scratch. That matters when you're trying to build more than another swap interface.

The tokenization side is worth understanding too. Trading perpetuals linked to real-world assets isn't the same as issuing the underlying assets, and neither is the same as maintaining official ownership records. Injective has been developing infrastructure across these different layers, including Injective Mint and SEC-registered transfer-agent capabilities. They're distinct functions, but together they matter for bringing more sophisticated financial products onchain.

Then there's the AI side. The MCP Server, Agent Skills, AI Agent SDK, x402 payments and Agent Platform are aimed at letting software agents interact with the network and carry out financial tasks. That opens up a different set of possibilities beyond humans manually clicking through trading apps.

Put all of that together and you start to see why I don't think the usual “DeFi chain” label tells the whole story.

Shared trading infrastructure, asset issuance, compliance tools and AI agents are all part of the picture. The question is whether adoption catches up with what is being built.

That's the part of Injective I think deserves a closer look.

$INJ 🥷

text:
Knowledge graphs for AI agents don’t need another database server.

KGLite is an embedded, Cypher-queryable knowledge graph for Python and Rust, built for applications, analysts, and LLM agents.

It helps you load and query structured context alongside your application by running the graph engine in-process, without an external database service.

Key features:

• In-process graph engine – runs inside your application instead of requiring a separate database service
• Cypher queries – query nodes and relationships with a Cypher interface from Python or Rust
• DataFrame loading – bulk-load nodes and relationships from pandas DataFrames
• Bundled MCP server – hand a saved graph file to an agent through the included MCP server
• Agent-aware schema – `describe()` returns a schema sized for an LLM prompt rather than a DBA

It’s open-source (MIT license).

Robinhood’s own print for a stock token follows a 24/5 session. Over the weekend it is held, and it stands still until 00:00 UTC on Monday.

None of those is called a basis.

A basis needs both prices live and no more than 10 minutes apart, and a held print is neither.

At this read the board stood behind a basis on 0 tokens, and it says why on every row.

𝟬𝟱. 𝗘𝗩𝗘𝗥𝗬 𝗧𝗢𝗞𝗘𝗡’𝗦 𝗩𝗘𝗥𝗗𝗜𝗖𝗧, 𝗜𝗡 𝗦𝗜𝗫 𝗪𝗢𝗥𝗗𝗦

Each token gets one verdict, checked in this order: halted, paused, unknown, held, stale, open.

→ halted: the issuer flags a halt in the stock
→ paused: a corporate action is in progress
→ unknown: no halt flag or no quote time to judge by
→ held: the session is closed, so the print stands still
→ stale: the print is older than this token’s own allowance
→ open: none of the above

The allowance is per token: 15 minutes times the 90th percentile of the last 48 gaps between its own prints, never under one and never over two of those 15 minutes.

At this read: 193 held, 1 open, 0 halted, 0 paused, 0 stale, 0 unknown.

text:
AI coding agents are starting to need documentation as infrastructure, not just context.
Google’s Developer Knowledge ecosystem now gives agents programmatic access to its official developer docs through an API, MCP server, CLI, agent skill and client libraries.
The important shift is architectural.
Instead of:
model → stale training data → code
the agent can run:
task → documentation retrieval → current source → code or decision
The same knowledge layer can serve an IDE agent, a CLI workflow or a production application.
Google’s latest updates make the system more usable: client libraries are available for seven languages, and AnswerQuery now uses Gemini 3.5 Flash.
For builders, I’d treat documentation retrieval as a first-class tool:
— search before generating implementation details
— retrieve the source page before making a consequential change
— preserve document references in the agent trace
— record when the source was retrieved and updated
— fall back to broader search when the required information is outside the corpus
— never treat “official docs” as proof that generated code is correct
The model still writes the code.
But the knowledge layer increasingly determines whether it is writing against the API that exists today.

text:
Closing keynote and a packed house after an extremely busy week at Team ’26 Europe in Amsterdam! From a Software Developer and Product perspective, this week was GOLD! The most valuable part of this week was proximity to problems.

Here are some huge takeaways:

- 15 MILLION+ MCP tool calls every day! Atlassian's MCP server just got a massive upgrade with 220 tools, expanding what developers and AI agents can access and accomplish across the Atlassian ecosystem.

- Loom can turn a screen recording into instructions for an AI agent. Instead of spending time explaining every visual change in a text prompt, developers can show what they want, talk through it, and have Loom generate structured instructions and acceptance criteria.

- Loom can also generate video walkthroughs of pull requests. It can run the previous and updated application, demonstrate what changed, explain implementation decisions, and show how the changes were tested. Think about how this changes code reviews as AI-generated PRs become more common.

- Atlassian built its new Artifacts application entirely on Forge! Not just a custom panel or extension. The UI, search, Teamwork Graph integration, Smart Links, and MCP tools were all built using Forge. If you've been wondering what you can actually build with Forge, this should expand your thinking.

- 250 BILLION+ objects and relationships in the Teamwork Graph. AI is only as useful as the context it can access. Connecting work, knowledge, code, people, and decisions gives agents a much better foundation to operate on.

- Up to 25% fewer tokens with the upgraded MCP server. More capabilities don't automatically have to mean higher token costs. How we design the infrastructure around our agents matters.

One thing became increasingly clear this week.
The conversation around AI development needs to move beyond which model you're using or how quickly you can generate code.

How are you giving agents the right context?
How are you making their work reviewable?
How are you connecting that work to the rest of your organization?

Those are engineering decisions, and they're becoming more important as AI adoption accelerates.

There's a LOT for Software Developers and builders to explore here!

Octocode is a Rust code-intelligence tool for builders who want MCP-compatible AI assistants to navigate a codebase.

It’s open-source (Apache License 2.0).

text:
One of the best parts of offering my AI Productivity course every 6 months is it gives me the opportunity to reflect on what exactly has changed in my AI workflows in that time.

Here's exactly how I'm updating my course to reflect those changes:

1. I previously trumpeted Claude Code as the most robust AI platform available. But now there is an entire category of agentic platforms, with ChatGPT's Codex being equally powerful and every other platform seeking to copy the capabilities, including Cursor, Grok Bot, Google's Antigravity, and GitHub Copilot.

2. I previously relied heavily on creating and managing local markdown files for context. But now, with robust MCP servers, I consider local markdown files an anti-pattern. I default to storing all my company context in a shared document repository with a robust MCP server. I use Notejoy, but Notion and Google Workspace are also great options.

3. The default artifact I previously generated was also markdown. But I've ultimately come to realize it's actually very limited in richness. I've now shifted to make much of my output HTML, giving me a far more expressive canvas for reports, dashboards, and more.

4. As AI slop becomes a real problem across teams deploying AI, I've taken to heart the need to teach explicitly how to apply your own judgment to AI output to  ensure you maintain accountability over it.

5. I previously taught how to simply automate a workflow. But now I teach how to ensure that workflow also compounds, ensuring the quality of output gets better with every single use.

6. I previously encouraged people to leverage their existing Figma design systems via the Figma MCP to ensure design consistency with prototypes. But now I encourage everyone to re-implement their design system in code, documented in Storybook, so that they have the highest level of consistency and enable their engineering team to accelerate converting those prototypes into production code.

7. I used to recommend many AI prototyping tools like Bolt, Replit, Lovable, etc. But now that teams are already using agentic platforms like Claude Code and Codex to automate workflows, I recommend using the same platform for prototyping.

8. I used to recommend platforms like Relay and Gumloop for automating complex workflows that required data from disparate sources, but now with powerful agentic platforms and robust MCP connections, it's just easier to rely on the platforms you are already heavily invested in (Claude Code or Codex).

9. I previously recommended double checking the output of any data analysis AI did on your behalf. But now with well established techniques of golden examples, adding a semantic layer, etc, you can now get to accuracy you can trust.

10. The majority of my AI usage lived in terminals and desktop apps. But Claude Tag has brought some of that directly into Slack.

text:
A few months ago, I published an article about building an MCP server with .NET.

And the most common response I got was:
“Can you record a video version of this?”
So I did.

But I didn’t want to make another generic “AI chatbot talks to your app” demo.

I wanted to show something more practical:
How can an AI agent actually interact with a real .NET application and help us understand what is happening at runtime?

The demo is simple.

I have an ASP. NET Core API with two endpoints:
/slow-thread-sleep
/slow-task-delay

At first glance, they look almost identical.

Both wait.
Both return a response.
Both seem fine from the outside.

But under load, they behave very differently.

So I built an MCP server in .NET that exposes a few tools the AI agent can use:
→ run a load test
→ compare the endpoints
→ analyze the results
→ generate a performance report

And this is where MCP becomes much more interesting.
The AI is no longer just reading code and guessing.

It can call real tools, collect real runtime data, and explain the behavior based on actual measurements.

That’s the part I think many developers are missing when they look at MCP.
MCP is not only about giving AI more context.

It’s about giving AI controlled access to useful actions inside your system.

That could be:
→ performance testing
→ logs
→ metrics
→ database diagnostics
→ deployment checks
→ feature flags
→ internal workflows

Or anything else your team needs.
I recorded a short video where I explain the concept and show the full demo in action.

Watch it here: https://t.co/3jy5D5zp2P

text:
Why GenLayer Has Spent More Than Two Years Building (A look at its testnets)

What if a contract could read real-world information, understand a written agreement, and help decide whether its terms have been met?

That is the problem @GenLayer  is working on. Its goal is to let software handle decisions that are too nuanced while making those decisions through a decentralized network.

GenLayer has been building in public since 2024. That means more than two years of steady work. This is not just adding an AI tool to an ordinary blockchain. The system must make AI-assisted decisions in a way that independent participants can verify, agree with, and challenge when needed.

Most blockchains are designed so every computer produces the same result when it runs the same instructions. That consistency is a strength. But real-world decisions are not always so tidy. A contract might need to interpret a written request, check information on the web, or decide whether something like “significantly delayed” has occurred. Different AI models can reach different conclusions. Web pages can change. And when money or agreements are involved, one AI’s answer is not enough.

GenLayer uses a process called Optimistic Democracy, where validators reach agreement using AI models and can escalate disputed decisions through appeals.

The three testnets

To prepare for mainnet, testnets were established. 

GenLayer’s path is Asimov → Bradbury → Clarke. Each stage has a clear purpose.

1.  Asimov – Building the foundation

Launched in June 2025, Asimov was the first public testnet. It was the first full rehearsal: could the network process contracts, assess outcomes, and reach agreement? It focused on validator onboarding, core network operations, and early tools for Intelligent Contracts.

2. Bradbury – Putting AI into the decision process

Bradbury shifts the focus to the AI models themselves. Validators, builders, and researchers experiment with different models, compare performance, and test how AI inference works alongside consensus. GenLayer describes it as a workshop rather than a finished product; performance can vary, and the network may be reset.

3. Clarke – Making the network safe

Clarke is the final testnet before mainnet. This stage is about economics and safety: proving the network can operate securely and sustainably under real economic conditions. It is the last major checkpoint before mainnet.

In one line

Asimov tested the foundations. Bradbury brought AI into the decision process. Clarke focuses on making the network safe and economically sound.

That is why the time matters. GenLayer is building a system where software can interpret real-world information and reach decisions through a decentralized process. Before people can rely on it, each layer has to be tested, challenged, and strengthened one stage at a time.

text:
Continuing today's memecoin recap series

Overall, market volume has improved quite a bit compared to the past few days, and several plays I've been watching recently have also been performing pretty well

Personally, I really like these kinds of setups. My trading style has always been focused on higher-cap plays with solid liquidity, a strong narrative, and clear catalysts, rather than constantly chasing low-cap gambles

And the first token I want to talk about today is solana:8nnaeWCw8mUypcGAgbmSuzAT85uWx4UN12adDrMhXrGF

I'm pretty sure most of you already know the story behind HOTBOT, so I won't spend too much time explaining its AI trading agent concept again

What I'm more interested in is what has actually changed over the past few days, why capital is starting to flow into HOTBOT, whether its current valuation still makes sense, and where I'd consider buying the dip

Let's break it down

1. Why wasn't I particularly interested in HOTBOT before?

HOTBOT isn't something that just appeared today

I'd been keeping an eye on it since its market cap was still relatively low, but back then, I didn't see enough reasons to put it on my high-conviction watchlist

The idea of building a private AI trading team was interesting

Instead of having a single chatbot generating trading signals, HOTBOT aims to combine ResearchBot, SniperBot, TraderBot, and LaunchBot into one system that can research tokens, identify entries, and execute trades based on strategies set by users

But at that stage, most of what I saw was still a concept, a litepaper, and a product with very limited beta access

I've researched quite a few AI agent projects, and one recurring problem is that the concept sounds great, but the actual product often struggles to live up to expectations

That's why I preferred to keep watching rather than ape in purely because of the narrative

Now, at least, HOTBOT has more concrete data for us to evaluate

2. What is the team actually building?

This is one of the developments I find most encouraging

Between October 5 and 10, @usehotbot consistently shared product updates

One of the most notable is ShieldBot, a system designed to filter out tokens showing signs of rugs or scams before they enter the trading pipeline

According to the team's internal data, ShieldBot can filter out more than 90% of risky tokens from a dataset of over 50K new tokens per day

Among the tokens that pass its filters, the team claims roughly 9 out of 10 picks have gone up, with around 70% reaching 3x or more

Those numbers sound impressive, but I want to emphasize that they're self-reported and haven't been independently verified

Another interesting update is Faster Data

The team says they've removed their reliance on certain third-party APIs and switched to pulling data directly on-chain, allowing their bots to detect new tokens roughly 60 seconds earlier than before

In memecoin trading, speed matters a lot, especially when some of the best opportunities only exist for a very short window

They've also introduced Smarter Settings and reportedly increased their research capacity to around 1,000 concurrent checks

I like seeing the team continuously improve the product, but its actual performance still needs to be proven as beta access expands

3. How credible is the team behind HOTBOT?

One thing I always check when researching AI projects is who's actually building the product

Based on the information shared publicly, HOTBOT has two main technical contributors :

@elijahintek, who is described as having previous experience with Gate and x402

@0xWhoismax, who is said to have previously worked with Light Terminal

The team emphasizes that both developers are doxxed and actively building in public

Personally, I see this as a positive because the community can at least follow the people responsible for developing the product

Another detail worth mentioning is the team's claim that the developer wallet primarily accumulated tokens through buybacks rather than holding a large allocation from launch

However, being doxxed doesn't automatically make a project safe

What matters more is whether the team keeps shipping, expands the product, and delivers on its tokenomics commitments

4. The tokenomics are what really caught my attention

Unlike many AI memecoins that rely almost entirely on narrative to attract capital, HOTBOT is trying to give its token an actual role within the product

According to the team's announced model :

Users are expected to stake around 50,000 HOTBOT to unlock product access, with a seven-day cooldown when unstaking

There's also a subscription fee of approximately $20 per month, payable in USDC or SOL, to maintain the private trading team and cover AI operating costs

TraderBot is designed to charge a 0.5% trading fee. Under the proposed mechanism, 100% of those fees would be used to buy HOTBOT from the market, with 60% of the purchased tokens burned and 40% allocated to the treasury

There's also Quant Mode, which would require burning around 25,000 HOTBOT to unlock more advanced research tools and strategy customization

If these mechanisms are fully implemented, HOTBOT could have multiple sources of token demand rather than relying entirely on speculation

But I still consider this tokenomics model a work in progress, not something already operating at scale

5. Creator fees and buybacks are starting to show meaningful numbers

This is probably the most important part of the current thesis

According to a ClawPump snapshot compiled on October 10, HOTBOT had generated approximately 627.5 SOL in cumulative creator fees

The same snapshot recorded around 252.4 SOL under buybacks, while nearly 79,950 $ANSEM had been distributed to holders, worth approximately $11K at the time

Previously, the team had also announced an airdrop of roughly 48,380 $ANSEM 

These figures suggest that token trading activity has already generated actual fees, with some value being distributed back to the community

However, there's something worth paying attention to

The creator fee allocation has been described differently across various updates

One snapshot showed 30% allocated to buybacks, 25% to holder airdrops, and 45% to the creator, while earlier announcements mentioned a 50/25/25 structure

That's why I'll continue monitoring the on-chain data rather than assuming one fixed allocation

More importantly, creator fees generated from token trading do not mean HOTBOT is already generating significant revenue from users of its AI trading product

Those are two different sources of value

6. Why has HOTBOT pumped so hard in such a short period?

I don't think there's one single catalyst behind HOTBOT's recent move

It's more likely the result of several factors coming together

First, the AI trading agent narrative is starting to attract attention again

Second, HOTBOT's connection to ClawPump and AnsemHack has helped it gain visibility within the Solana community

Third, the team has been consistently shipping updates while many projects in the same category are still stuck at the idea stage

And finally, the creator fee, buyback, and holder reward mechanisms have started getting people interested in the possibility of a sustainable flywheel

The logic is pretty straightforward

More attention can lead to higher token trading volume, which generates more creator fees, with a portion potentially going toward buybacks or holder distributions

If the product eventually attracts real users, bot trading fees could become an additional source of demand

But I think it's important to separate these two flywheels

The first one depends heavily on speculative memecoin trading volume

The second depends on the product's ability to attract and retain actual users

Right now, we have data supporting the first one

The second still needs to prove itself

7. What does the on-chain data tell us?

Based on the latest figures I've reviewed, HOTBOT has approximately 5.2K–5.6K holders, a significant increase from its early days

The top 10 holders reportedly control around 23–24% of the supply, depending on the snapshot and whether system wallets are excluded

Several token security tools have also given relatively positive assessments of basic security factors such as mint authority, freeze authority, and liquidity status

However, I wouldn't consider a high security score enough to conclude that a token is safe

HOTBOT is only around eight days old, its holder history is still very limited, and liquidity remains relatively thin compared to its valuation

Some reports put liquidity around $300K–$800K while market cap has already reached approximately $6–7M

That means a large wave of profit-taking could easily trigger a sharp correction

For me, the next thing to watch isn't just whether the holder count continues increasing

It's also whether major wallets are accumulating, distributing, or moving their tokens elsewhere

8. What are the next catalysts?

I think HOTBOT has already benefited from the initial attention surrounding AnsemHack and ClawPump

So I wouldn't expect an old hackathon announcement to remain the main driver of price action

The most important catalyst now is broader product access

HOTBOT is still primarily operating under an invite-only model

If the team successfully expands beta access, attracts real users, and starts publishing verifiable trading data, the thesis could become significantly stronger

There are three things I particularly want to see

First, the actual number of active users, not just people signing up for a waitlist

Second, trading volume and fees generated by the product itself, rather than creator fees from token speculation

And finally, independently verifiable bot performance data, including losing trades

If HOTBOT can deliver on these points, the market may eventually start valuing it as a trading software business with an associated token, rather than just another AI memecoin

If not, the current narrative could lose momentum pretty quickly

9. Chart analysis and my dip-buying plan

Now let's look at the H1 chart 

HOTBOT spent a relatively long period consolidating around the $1–2M market cap range before breaking out aggressively

It then expanded toward $6–7M, briefly wicked close to $9M, and pulled back toward $6.5M

The positive part is that the breakout came with a noticeable increase in volume, suggesting that fresh capital was entering the market

But after such an aggressive move, I'm not interested in chasing green candles

My plan is pretty simple

$5–5.5M MC: This is the first area where I'd watch for a reaction. If price pulls back here, selling volume starts declining, and buyers show signs of absorbing supply, I may consider opening a small position

$4–5M MC: This is the area I find more attractive from a risk/reward perspective if we get a deeper pullback. However, I'd only consider adding if the price structure starts stabilizing, not simply because the token has dropped significantly

$2.5–3.5M MC: This would be a deeper correction scenario if momentum fades or the market starts losing confidence in the narrative. If HOTBOT returns to this range, I'd reassess the thesis rather than automatically treating it as a bargain

As for invalidation, if HOTBOT loses the $4M region and fails to reclaim it while selling volume increases, I'd avoid aggressive DCA and prioritize capital preservation

On the other hand, if price consolidates well around $6M and eventually breaks above the $8–9M region with strong volume, HOTBOT could enter another phase of price discovery

Even then, I'd still prefer waiting for a retest rather than FOMOing directly into the breakout

These are areas I'm watching based on the current chart structure, not guaranteed support levels

10. Bull case, bear case, and my final thoughts

I think HOTBOT is one of the more interesting AI trading agent projects to watch on Solana right now

My bull case isn't based on the team claiming ShieldBot has an extremely high win rate or that its AI can consistently identify 3x tokens

What interests me is whether HOTBOT can turn an AI trading product into an ecosystem with real users, real revenue, and mechanisms that create actual demand for its token

If the team continues shipping, successfully expands beta access, grows its active user base, and sustains buybacks through recurring fees, the current valuation could still have room to grow

But the bear case is just as clear

The product is still invite-only, its AI performance hasn't been independently verified, several tokenomics mechanisms aren't fully operational yet, and much of the current valuation still depends on narrative and speculative trading volume

At a $6–7M market cap, HOTBOT is no longer as cheap as it was in its early stages

The market has already started pricing in future expectations, while the project still has plenty left to prove

Personally, I like the direction the team is taking, and I think HOTBOT has more substance than most AI memecoins I've researched

But liking a project doesn't mean I need to buy it at any price

I'll continue monitoring creator fees, buyback activity, product updates, and most importantly, actual adoption

If we get a decent dip into the areas I'm watching and the thesis remains intact, I'll consider taking a position

For now, I see no reason to FOMO after a move of several hundred percent

Even a good project can be a bad trade if you enter at the wrong price

That's how I'm looking at HOTBOT right now

Matthew Berman had Claude Opus 5.5 recreate San Francisco in Unreal Engine...

the trick is splitting the work: Opus builds the city, Jev runs the life inside it, but there's a smart way to set it up:

- step 2: feed it real city data: building footprints, heights, the street grid
- step 3: Opus generates the city block by block: downtown towers, parks, the bay, the bridge
- step 4: add the life: pedestrians, pets, cars, buses on real streets
- step 5: every agent asks Jev a quick question: cross now or wait? which lane? where next?
- step 6: Jev answers in under a second for fractions of a cent, so thousands of agents can decide on their own
- step 7: build and check one district at a time, then fly the camera out over the whole city

and that's why it works at this scale...

a reasoning model is too slow and too expensive to decide for thousands of cars
a decision model was built for exactly that

Opus builds, Jev decides

Anthropic just published the 𝗳𝘂𝗹𝗹 𝗼𝗳𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗱𝗼𝗰𝘀 for dynamic workflows in Managed Agents. They planted 70 bugs in a 116K-line codebase. Across three runs, a single agent found 14, 15 and 27. A Managed Agents workflow ran three times and 𝗳𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱 𝟲𝟲 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲. You can have Opus 5.5 follow the docs to go through your project, pick the job most worth splitting across many agents, and run it as a dynamic workflow in Claude Code.

In a dynamic workflow, Claude writes the plan first, hands the work to many agents in phases, then combines the results. Managed Agents bills at API rates. Claude Code has dynamic workflows too, on 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝗽𝗮𝗶𝗱 𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗻, and they count toward your plan's usage (on Pro, turn them on in /config first). A single run can send out up to 1,000 agents, and every one of them uses your limits, so start with one directory. /workflows shows how many tokens each agent has used, and you can stop the run at any time.

Send this prompt to Opus 5.5 👇

"Read these two docs:
https://t.co/8dh6t8t6Bq
https://t.co/gMdIOeiSEK
We'll run this as a dynamic workflow in Claude Code. From the second doc, only borrow how it splits and reviews the work.

Then go through this project's code, issues and recent commits, and find three kinds of work that fit a dynamic workflow:
1. Checks that need to cover the whole repo, like hunting for bugs or finding missing permission checks.
2. Migrations that touch many files, like moving from JavaScript to TypeScript.
3. Fixes you have to repeat until they pass, like a pile of type-check errors. Stop if two rounds in a row make no progress.
If the project doesn't have one of these, just say so. Don't force it.

Pick the one most worth doing and plan it on a single directory first, with no more than 10 agents for now. Give each piece of work one agent, and pair each piece with a second agent that reviews it and looks for what the first one missed. One agent failing must not fail the whole run; list anything that didn't get covered. If you pick a check, hand every issue it reports to another agent to pick apart, and only count the ones that hold up.

Show me in writing which one you picked, how many phases it has and how many agents it sends out. Don't start the workflow or change any files until I confirm."

Fable 5.1 reads the whole session, every tool call included, and steps in at three moments:

-> before a plan: is this the right approach?
-> when the same error keeps coming back: am I digging in the wrong place?

the clever part: toggling /advisor leaves the Opus prompt cache intact, so you only pay for the few moments Fable actually reads the session

text:
Free Claude Code, Codex and Cursor from Kickbacks: is everything people say true, and what does it actually pay 

Kickbacks puts ads in Claude Code's loading line and promises a revenue share. The hype hit all of X and Hacker News. I took the main promises and checked them against the FAQ, the terms, code teardowns and reports from people who installed it

1. "It pays you for ads in Claude Code" – true

While the agent thinks, a sponsored line replaces "thinking…". Advertisers buy blocks of 1,000 impressions at auction, bids start at $0.50 per block. An impression counts after 10 seconds of continuous screen time

2. "It works in Cursor" – half true

The extension installs in Cursor, but it only pays for Claude Code and Codex running inside it. Cursor's own agent shows no ads. Codex in the terminal earns nothing. Claude Code in the terminal only earns if the VS Code extension is installed too

3. "Half the revenue is yours" – half true

Launch promised an honest 50/50. The FAQ now says "an estimated 50% of the net ad revenue", meaning after their costs. The rate and payouts can change with a notice on the site

4. "It pays for your subscription" – no

The numbers are all over the place:
· founder in July: $25/month on average, top 10% at $75
· Kickbacks' own terms: ~$75 per user per year
· real reports: $0.43 for a full workday, $4.43 for 3 hours (407 impressions), $10 for 2 hours
Even the most generous figure is $25 against $200 for Claude Max. A discount, yes. Free Claude, no

5. "You can farm it" – no

Only real prompts you started yourself count. Sub-agent waits don't count, there are daily caps and one account per person. Scripts and bots get payouts voided and the account banned

6. "Anthropic won't ban you" – nobody knows

Anthropic has nothing to do with it. The extension patches the official Claude Code bundle, loosens its CSP (that stays until a full uninstall) and auto-updates from its own servers outside the marketplace. Kickbacks' own terms say the provider may block your account and they take no responsibility. There's precedent: OpenCode dropped Claude sign-in after legal requests from Anthropic

7. "Your code never leaves your machine" – true, until you turn on Boosted

Private Mode is the default: the ad network gets a pseudonymous ID, city, OS and editor version. Boosted Mode promises up to 5x CPM but sends chunks of your prompts and responses to their server for targeting

And the detail nobody mentions: payouts are Stripe Connect only, roughly every 2 weeks, $10 minimum

Verdict

This isn't free Claude. It's a couple of dollars a week for ads in your editor, plus an account risk nobody takes responsibility for. If you want to try it, use a secondary account, keep Private Mode on and don't expect it to cover your subscription

Install with one command: npx -y @kickbacksai/install

text:
A credit system for AI agents needs to know when to stop trusting a good track record.

That's where @agenticscredit multi-agent risk model gets interesting.

Each agent has its own ACS, but an operator running several agents also gets a holistic score weighted by capital allocation.

If that combined score falls too far, every credit line can be paused, not just the one attached to the weakest agent.

I think this addresses a real blind spot in evaluating autonomous trading systems.

An operator might have one strategy performing well while another accumulates losses. Looking at each agent in isolation can miss the risk building across the whole operation.

A portfolio-level score offers a broader view.

But the key test is whether the aggregation reflects the risks that actually matter, especially when strategies behave differently under changing market conditions.

Scoring individual agents is one challenge.

Managing the combined exposure is another.

text:
Five bots can still leave you with one big bet

Imagine several agents using different entry signals while all staying long BTC. Their names and trading rules differ, but a sharp sell-off could hurt them together.

That’s the portfolio question I bring to @agenticscredit multi-agent setup. Its whitepaper describes combining individual ACS ratings into a capital-weighted score for the operator.

Looking across the whole account makes sense. But a combined rating alone doesn’t tell me how much the strategies overlap.

I’d want to see shared positions, total directional exposure, and how often the agents lose at the same time. The published rollup description doesn’t establish how those relationships are measured.

Before adding another bot, I’d ask what risk it actually changes in the portfolio.

*update 18 months later*

if i was starting a PhD in AI this year (or a neolab...), i would work on civilization-tier simulations 

I am convinced that (a) the timing is right, (b) there are interesting/fun research problems, (c) these will be the core research questions of ~2028-30+

why/why now: 

(1) the trend is increasingly more compute per problem (low-latency response -> cot -> deep research -> agent -> multi-agent). what does this look like in the limit? how do we go from 1 agent -> 10 agents -> 1 million agents working on a single task?

while not everything needs that level of scale - surely, some problems (e.g., discovery/research, forecasting, storytelling) will benefit. 

and as we scale, the surface area for research only increases. more opportunities for inductive biases, more risk of misalignment, more wasted/redundant compute that can be regularized/repurposed.

when you're scaling layers or training flops, you cant necessarily observe/understand/doctor specific aspects of your scaled system. but you can when you're scaling multi-agent systems

(2) parallel advancements in other technologies have/will enable us to align to the real world in increasingly richer ways. 

for example, wearables/ml for deriving emotional signal from sensors should see massive advancements once they start doing agent-supported surveys + personalized fine-tuning. and if you can (even noisily) collect data on someones emotional state across time -- how would you build a civilization-tier simulation to model it? (ones own version of inside out)

or with the power of agent-driven surveying/data analysis, we will be able to meaningfully collect signals that will let us better model entire populations.

(3) while the jury is still out on whether rsi will break free of the curse of jagged intelligence, it is a certainty that the cost of current capabilities will get much cheaper/faster

what happens when the cost of running 1K parallel fable-tier agents is < $1? what about 1M agents? todays models wont trivially cooperate/benefit from that scale

and everything will be so much faster too! what if latency drops to < 1s for complex tasks? what if you can run 1K agents for real-time video generation?

and when you factor in fine-tuned/cheaper models, balancing/routing across the pareto frontier, human-in-the-loop -- it becomes clear how many challenges open up around steering societies/civilizations of agents
---------------
what/where's the impact:

(1) pushing the frontier/discovery, complex modeling, better systems

how do you productively scale agents to 1M scientists for biology research? how do you ensure they cover the search space in a productive way? do you simulate peer-review within your simulation? do you have an auction for limited real-world resources (eg for validating)?

and there are some systems that are so complex (eg stock market) that they should surely benefit from infinitely scaling agents (especially since data/real-world signal will scale too). 

it will be non-trivial to build such systems, both in the design of architectures (even multi-agent architecture is clearly unsolved), learning methods (even multi-agent learning is barely being on worked on), gradient-based learning methods (e.g., how do you RL to be more useful for large-scale multi-agent/civilization-tier systems)

(2) human-alignment (entertainment, education, modeling)

with (i) increase in real-world signals (better sensors, better surveys, better telemetry), (ii) increase in real-world surfaces/mediums (video, vr, increasingly immersive modalities), (iii) extremely speed-up to enable real-time processing -- so much is possible

what is the limit of storytelling if you can dynamically steer/generate video based on feedback from real world sensors? how do you build civilization-scale multi-agent systems to do this?

what about negotiation/sales? or advertising/marketing? or education? the promise of personalized education makes me so hopeful for the future -- imagine being able to scale (on both the detection/tracking/teaching/etc) precisely optimize for fun + productive education. imagine creating rich simulations of competitive environments to induce better learning.

just as scientific research/complex systems (point 1) and user modeling (point 2) would benefit from scaling up systems, its only natural that to best model a population of humans -- there is value to scaling up the number of agents

text:
Why have ONE Hermes bot handle an entire project when you can have a team of specialized bots working together?

One AI agent can do a lot. But when you're working on a complex project, there's a real advantage to dividing the work among specialists that can communicate, collaborate, and coordinate everything from planning through execution.

Here's why this approach is worth considering:

• Specialization: Each bot focuses on a specific responsibility, with the right tools and a suitable model for its role.

• Collaboration: Bots can exchange ideas, share findings, and work through decisions together.

• Delegation: Responsibilities are distributed across the team instead of having one agent manage every part of the project.

• Parallel execution: Independent tasks can move forward at the same time.

• Review: One bot can evaluate another's work, identify problems, and send it back for improvements.

**How would you structure a team like this?**

Start with the project itself. Define what you're trying to accomplish, identify the specialties required, and give each bot a clear role.

Then establish how they'll communicate, share context, hand off tasks, and review one another's work.

For example, let's say you're building a simple task management app:

1. Planning Bot: Defines the requirements, features, and overall structure.
2. Development Bot: Writes the code and builds the functionality.
3. UI/UX Bot: Designs the interface and user experience.
4. Testing Bot: Checks the app, identifies issues, and sends feedback to the team.

The planning bot helps establish the direction. Development and design coordinate as the app takes shape. Testing identifies problems that get routed back for fixes.

The result is a coordinated workflow with specialized responsibilities, rather than one agent trying to handle everything.

Of course, not every task needs a team of bots. But when a project involves different specialties, multiple workstreams, and ongoing review, this approach makes a lot of sense.

text:
“The most trustworthy Super Intelligence system will not be the one with the model we trust most. It will be the one that enables us to trust the model the least.”

This is exactly the principle at @origin_trail's core: put knowledge and its provenance outside the model, where they can be shared, inspected and independently verified.

@satyanadella’s argument gets to the heart of trustworthy AI. A more capable model should not become the sole authority on what is true, or the sole witness to its own work.

Consider what this means as agents take on more responsibility:

→ Supply chains: An agent recommends switching suppliers. Show the certifications, capacity records and delivery history behind its recommendation—not just a persuasive summary.

→ Healthcare: An agent summarizes clinical evidence. Connect its claims to the original studies, their publication dates and the guidelines used. Let a clinician examine whether the evidence actually supports the conclusion.

→ Manufacturing: An agent recommends replacing a component. Trace the recommendation to sensor readings, maintenance records and the relevant technical specification.

→ Insurance: An agent assesses a claim. Make the policy version, inspection report and supporting documents available for review. Separate documented facts from the model’s interpretation.

→ Energy: An agent compares the emissions of two products. Expose the measurements, reporting boundaries and calculation methods—not just two numbers presented as equivalent.

→ Finance: An agent flags a company’s exposure to risk. Link the finding to dated disclosures and source records, so an analyst can distinguish new evidence from an outdated assumption.

→ Research: An agent proposes a new hypothesis. Preserve the distinction between published findings, derived conclusions and speculation. A citation is a starting point for verification, not proof by itself.

→ Multi-agent collaboration: One agent passes a finding to another. Carry the source and provenance with it, so repetition across agents doesn’t turn an unsupported claim into an accepted fact.

These workflows need more than a larger context window. They need a knowledge layer that persists across models and makes the supporting evidence accessible.

That is where Decentralized Knowledge Graph fits: connecting knowledge through explicit relationships, enabling shared context across agents, and providing provenance and verifiable integrity for published Knowledge Assets.

The distinction matters: verifying who published a record and whether it has changed does not prove the record is true. It gives people and systems a stronger basis for checking it.

Nor does a knowledge graph replace permissions, containment or human oversight. It complements them with evidence that does not depend on trusting the model’s explanation.

Better models can generate better answers. Better knowledge infrastructure lets us challenge those answers.

That is the future we’re building toward: AI grounded in verifiable knowledge, with provenance that can be checked independently of the model.

More intelligence demands more accountability. Not more blind trust.

Don’t just trust AI. Verify what it builds on.

text:
Sui’s Basecamp 2026 framed the chain not as another high-through put Layer 1 competing on raw consensus speed, but as a programmable trust layer for an economy in which most transactions are executed by software agents rather than people. 

The event October 7–8 at Marina Bay Sands, Singapore, alongside TOKEN2049 centered on that claim through a live demonstration of programmable off-chain tunnels reaching a reported peak of 40,614,180 transactions per second.

The introduction of @SuiNetwork  Agent Pass for bounded agent authority, progress on Hashi’s Bitcoin collateral system with more than $500 million in committed capital, and adjacent integrations such as Samsung Wallet support for USDC on Sui and Circle’s CCTP V2.

The tunnels result is the clearest technical illustration of the architectural bet. 

Sui tunnels function as programmable state and payment channels, analogous to Lightning Network channels but generalized beyond simple payments. 

Parties open a tunnel with an on-chain transaction that establishes rules, deposits, and verification parameters; they then exchange an arbitrary number of signed state updates off-chain.

Covering chat, games, micropayments, or agent-to-agent commerce in the demo and they close with a mutually cosigned settlement that is independently verifiable on Sui mainnet. 

Only the open and close hit the base layer. During the Summit Stage demonstration, more than 10,000 such tunnels opened on mainnet within seconds, with activity spanning payments, games, and chat, all gasless while open. 

CertiK observed the run in real time and was to publish a fuller review of proofs, logs, and settlement data.

This is not a claim that Sui’s validators processed 40 million discrete transactions per second. 

Real-time on-chain throughput on mainnet remains orders of magnitude lower; the headline figure measures activity inside the tunnels. 

The distinction is intentional. 

Adeniyi Abiodun, Mysten Labs co-founder and chief product officer, put it directly in an agentic economy Sui does not need to process every interaction; it needs to be the trust layer for them. 

Agents agree on rules at open, interact privately and rapidly in between, and settle or dispute on-chain. 

At machine scale, continuous on-chain fees would be prohibitive; two on-chain transactions per session keep intermediate costs near zero while preserving cryptographic finality and dispute resolution. 

The July 4, 2026 precursor had reached roughly 6.1 million TPS under similar conditions the Basecamp run was more than six times that and roughly double the 20 million target set for the event.

The design choices address practical constraints of agent commerce. 

AI agents already outnumber humans in some estimates and can generate high-frequency, low-value interactions API calls, game moves, continuous settlement of compute or data that human markets never produce. 

Abiodun has noted that no human market requires 6 million or 40 million TPS; agents do. 

Tunnels also support offline or low-connectivity use and selective privacy, with the final settlement and any disputes remaining auditable. 

Builders can design application-specific tunnels rather than being limited to payment logic. 

Earlier technical discussions around Sui’s approach including ZK-flavored generalizations of state channels emphasize that throughput is bounded by signing speed rather than consensus once the channel is open.

Complementing the throughput primitive is control over agent authority. 

Sui Agent Pass, introduced on the second day, is an on-chain mechanism that lets a user define bounded permissions for an agent or agent-controlled account: which assets or objects it can touch, spending or action limits, permitted counterparties, and revocable policies. 

The pitch is explicit “don’t trust the agent; trust the rules. 

Worst-case loss is capped by the pre-set bounds even if the agent’s key is compromised. 

Related “Rooms” provide shared, protocol-enforced environments for multi-party or multi-agent coordination for example, sealed bids or one-time purchase limits where rules are enforced by the chain rather than by agent goodwill. 

These were described as targeting Q4 2026 availability and as extending beyond simple coin allowances to non-coin objects and broader action sets. 

Evan Cheng and Abiodun framed this as addressing the binary of full wallet delegation versus no autonomy at all.

Adjacent announcements reinforce the same stack. Hashi, Sui’s Bitcoin collateral primitive, is moving to a phased mainnet rollout later in October.

With more than $500 million in capital commitments from a coalition of more than 20 partners including Anchorage Digital as a day-one institutional launch partner, plus vault providers such as Aftermath, Concrete, and Fluid, and names such as BitGo.

Native BTC stays on Bitcoin; an hBTC representation is minted on Sui against it for use in lending, credit, vaults, and structured products; burning hBTC releases the BTC. 

Security involves 2-of-2 multisig elements, a Guardian Layer, MPC, formal verification Certora and cryptographic review CommonPrefix.

The goal is productive use of idle Bitcoin without requiring its sale or movement off its native chain. 

Samsung Wallet integration targets native USDC on Sui for roughly 82 million eligible U.S. 

Galaxy devices launch aimed for late October while CCTP V2 enables native USDC movement between Sui and other supported chains. 

Alibaba Cloud collaboration points toward agent-driven payments for cloud and AI services under predefined budgets.

Taken together, these pieces describe a layered model: high-frequency off-chain interaction inside verifiable tunnels, on-chain settlement and dispute resolution, explicit policy bounds via Agent Pass, institutional-grade collateral via Hashi, and distribution through wallets and cloud providers. 

Sui’s object-centric model and Move language are positioned as advantages for fine-grained ownership and programmable rules that agents can both respect and be constrained by. 

Partnerships with Google prior Agentic Payments Protocol work and Verifiable Agent Arbiter concepts and cloud providers further orient the system toward machine to machine payments and auditable agent actions.

Caveats are material. 

The 40 million figure is off-chain tunnel activity, not sustained mainnet consensus throughput; independent analyses of earlier similar tests placed ordinary on-chain peaks far lower. 

Full CertiK reporting was still pending at announcement. 

Agent Pass and related controls were newly introduced and not yet generally available. 

Hashi’s capital is committed rather than necessarily deposited and active; the rollout is phased. 

Real adoption of agent commerce at scale remains prospective dependent on reliable agent tooling, regulatory clarity around autonomous payments, and whether builders actually use the tunnel primitives for production workloads rather than demos. 

Comparisons to Lightning are apt for the channel model but incomplete: Sui’s programmability expands the surface, yet it also expands the complexity of verification and dispute handling.

The deeper claim is that blockchains optimized solely for human transaction rates will be mismatched to an environment in which software continuously negotiates, pays for compute, settles game state, or coordinates across services. 

Basecamp’s demonstrations treat Sui’s role as that of a court and control plane final, programmable, and selective rather than a real-time processor of every agent message. 

Whether the combination of tunnels, bounded agent permissions, and Bitcoin collateral infrastructure proves sufficient for that role will be determined by subsequent mainnet usage, audit outcomes, and the emergence of applications that actually require machine-scale interaction under cryptographic rules. 

The event itself was an argument, in live numbers and product announcements, that the infrastructure layer should be built for the agents first.

text:
Some of you are building entire org charts of AI agents before figuring out how to make ONE agent reliable.

And the research is getting pretty uncomfortable.

Anthropic just disclosed that during internal testing, Claude submitted a fabricated homicide tip to an actual police website. It was caught as spam.

In other cases, agents submitted real forms instead of practice versions and worked around access restrictions to finish tasks.

Meanwhile, Google Research tested 180 agent configurations and found something interesting:

-> Multi-agent systems performed 39–70% worse on sequential planning tasks.

-> Independent agents amplified errors by up to 17.2x.

To be fair, orchestration DID improve performance on parallelizable tasks.

But here's what bothers me.

We're essentially rebuilding distributed systems, except now every service can confidently misunderstand the request and pass that misunderstanding to the next one. 

And the tragedy is most don't know how to reconstruct or backtrack exactly where a bad decision originated? They would ask the same system with a stupid prompt to "figure it out".

We've spent decades solving these problems in conventional software engineering.

Somehow, adding an LLM to the equation has convinced people that all problems will be magically taken care of.

text:
The first thing worth checking on @agenticscredit is your Agentic Credit Score, not a deposit screen.

Connect the wallet you already trade with at https://t.co/Y8JSbUiQxS. The platform reads your trading history and generates an ACS between 300 and 850, based on observable activity rather than a self-reported win rate.

An empty or limited wallet history returns Unrated. It means there is not enough closed trading activity to establish a score yet.

Once a record exists, your ACS falls into one of five bands:

• 740–850: Elite
• 670–739: Qualified
• 580–669: Emerging
• 300–579: Speculative
• Unrated: Insufficient history

The key threshold is 580.

At 580 or above, you qualify to join the funding waitlist for potential credit allocation. Below 580, you remain on the paper-trading path while working to improve your record. Reaching the threshold does not guarantee immediate funding.

What makes the scoring model worth understanding is how it combines different types of activity.

ACS considers paper trades executed through its engine alongside real onchain trading history, with real-money activity carrying greater weight. Paper trading helps build a record, but it does not erase weaknesses in your live performance.

Your score updates as positions close, making it an evolving assessment of your trading behavior rather than a one-time achievement.

There is also a risk-management layer. If credit is allocated, it is deployed through Agentics wallets to approved venues rather than sent directly to your personal wallet. The initial venue is Avantis perps on Base, with position limits, leverage restrictions, stop-loss controls, and drawdown safeguards.

Meanwhile, eligible closed trading activity also contributes to $CREDIT toward the upcoming user airdrop. Its monetary value and individual allocations have not been guaranteed.

Another detail worth noting is multi-agent scoring. Each agent develops its own record, while their performance contributes to a combined ACS. If the overall score falls far enough, credit lines linked to the account are paused together.

The process is straightforward:

Connect your wallet. Build a verifiable trading record. Track your ACS. Work toward the 580 threshold. Earn $CREDIT through eligible activity along the way.

For me, the important distinction is between earning a score, qualifying for a waitlist, and receiving actual capital. They are separate stages.

Check your trading record here: https://t.co/Y8JSbUiQxS

text:
Prompt engineering stopped being about writing the prompt, the deliverable now is the eval suite that proves it works

Most people still ship a prompt because it looked good on three examples, with nothing underneath to catch it drifting.

This lab flips the order, the test gets written first and no prompt leaves until it has survived an attack:

→ Ask: the goal and the failure modes go in before a single instruction
→ Examples: 48 cases locked as the baseline, 5 samples each
→ Variants: p1 and p2 behind one switch, run on all 48, count wins not vibes
→ Attack: 10 injections fired at both, anything that bends gets rewritten

• Why the test comes first
> A prompt with no eval is a demo, not a deliverable
> Every prompt lives in git, one diff per change
> A regression points at one line instead of a vague feeling

• The team inside it
> One lead agent holds the permanent rules in its system prompt
> Fast agents spawn per task in their own sandboxes
> They run tests and never write the prompt, so nobody grades their own work

• The knobs you actually tune
> Temperature, few-shot k, max tokens, output format
> All live sliders, so behaviour changes with no model round trip
> Budget split across system, examples and output, visible at all times

One full lab run, 48 cases by 5 samples plus 10 attacks, lands near $0.60.

And the part that broke my brain:

A clever prompt passed every demo I gave it.
The same prompt failed 11 of 48 cases the moment it was scored.

Same words. One of them had been tested.

The deliverable was never the prompt.

The prompt is below, copy it and run your own lab ↓
