text:
Do yourself a favor if you're serious about AI Engineering:

– Learn LLM APIs, tool calling, structured outputs and context engineering

– Find one boring, repetitive task people genuinely hate doing

– Check if simple automation can solve it before building an agent

– Define what success looks like before writing code

– Build one useful agent, not a team of 10 agents talking to each other

– Give it the right tools, context and memory only when needed

– Learn MCP, but use it when it actually makes integrations easier

– Build a small eval dataset from real examples before obsessing over prompts

– Test messy inputs, edge cases and failure scenarios, not just happy paths

– Validate tool inputs and outputs with strict schemas

– Make the agent verify its work instead of confidently guessing

– Teach it when to ask questions, stop or hand control back to a human

– Give tools minimum permissions and keep user data isolated

– Keep API keys and sensitive data out of prompts and logs

– Treat websites, documents and tool responses as untrusted input

– Sandbox risky execution and require approval before sending, spending or deleting

– Add timeouts, limited retries and safeguards against duplicate actions

– Save progress so long-running tasks can recover from failures

– Set limits on tokens, execution time and cost per task

– Use smaller models for easy tasks and reasoning models when needed, based on eval results

– Cache safe, repeatable work without serving stale or private data

– Trace model calls, tool usage, errors and decisions so you can debug failures

– Evaluate both the final answer and the steps the agent took

– Track task success rate, latency and cost per completed task

– Run evals in CI and block changes that break existing behavior

– Test new models and prompts on a small percentage of traffic before rolling them out

– Add fallbacks and a rollback plan for when models or tools fail

– Turn every real user complaint into a new test case

– Show users progress, clear errors and what the agent actually completed

– Deploy it with a live link people can genuinely try

– Write a simple README explaining how it works and its limitations

– Record a 60-second demo showing a real problem getting solved

text:
looking at pstack by @poteto and it's a goldmine of prompt engineering 

even her example prompt is the best template i've seen of the four things you need to give your agent in a single prompt:

* a goal
* a checkable finish condition
* the evidence you want to see
* constraints

I'm always surprised by how short pro's prompts are. It's less about length, but ensuring your hitting those four points. 

Here's the prompt:

/poteto-mode fix the duplicate notification after retry.
Reproduce it first. Done means retrying produces exactly one notification and normal delivery still works.
Show the failing and passing evidence. Leave a PR for review.

So simple

define what you want, how to know when you're done, what you want to see, and what you shouldn't do

I guarantee you this isn't obvious to most prompters

text:
you’re paying Opus $20 per million tokens to answer yes or no questions

most of an agent loop isn’t coding.

it’s deciding.

→ Opus 5.5 plans and writes the code
→ Jev answers every yes/no, pick one, rank it
→ plain code acts on the probability
→ Opus only wakes up when Jev isn’t sure

Opus writes. Jev decides.

paste this into claude code 👇

claude plugin marketplace add typesafe-ai/skills
claude plugin install typesafe@typesafe-ai

Rebuild my agent loop as: Opus writes, Jev decides, code acts.
1. Find every place my agent asks a model a yes/no, pick one, or rank question (routing, "is this done?", "is this safe?", retries).
2. Replace each with one Jev call (model: jev-latest) that returns probabilities. Output is free, so ask all the questions in a single call.
3. Put the thresholds in plain code. Low confidence escalates to Opus 5.5, never down.
4. Log every Jev call and every escalation so I can see the savings.
Show me the diff before changing anything.

I have a few global agent loop builds under my belt now and the biggest discovery I found has been

Strip out as much complexity as you can

Give the agents clear tool primitives and reduce the number of tools they need to use where possible (deduplicate tools and instead add more parameters into the tool)

text:
Elon Musk just wrote and published a 12-page PDF on turning Grok Bot into an AI memory engine that remembers projects without drowning in chat history.

It is more useful than most paid AI-agent courses:

step 1 → stop calling a giant chat log memory. If your Bot remembers yesterday's answer but not why it was true, it will confidently repeat a dead fact.

step 2 → split the stack into active context, durable memory, a task checkpoint and live sources. They answer four different questions; one mega-summary cannot do all four.

step 3 → put a write gate in front of memory. Save approved decisions and reusable lessons; reject guesses, scraped instructions and random sentences from old chats.

step 4 → give every saved claim a receipt: type, scope, source, owner, time, audience and the event that makes it stale.

step 5 → version corrections. When a deadline moves, mark the old one superseded and build a clean current view instead of feeding both dates back to Grok Bot.

step 6 → filter memory by permission, project and validity before similarity search. A 0.99 match is useless if the record belongs to someone else.

step 7 → build a lean run packet: current task, boundaries, checkpoint, selected memory IDs, fresh evidence and open questions. Stop pasting the entire conversation.

step 8 → reopen the world. Memory can point to CI, tickets and approvals; it cannot prove that today's build passed or grant permission to deploy.

step 9 → checkpoint before compaction. Keep the goal, hard constraints, finished work, blockers, source links and next safe action so a fresh session can actually continue.

step 10 → make old memory die. Supersede decisions, expire observations and delete records that should never have been stored.

step 11 → scope memory across the team. Share approved process; keep private facts private; hand off evidence instead of entire chats.

step 12 → test the whole loop across sessions: write, retrieve, correct, recheck, resume and stay inside the approval boundary. A trivia answer is not a memory system.

the result: Grok Bot stops acting like a chat with a long autobiography and starts acting like an agent that knows what to keep, what to load, what to verify and when to forget.

🧵 Verifiable Knowledge: The Third Pillar of Trust for Agentic AI

An AI agent can act on your behalf.

But where did its knowledge come from?
Was it altered?
Was it authorized to use it?

@EQTYLab is building infrastructure to make those questions verifiable. 👇

On June 1, 2026, EQTY introduced Verifiable Knowledge, extending its work with @nvidia 

The architecture now spans three pillars:

• Verifiable Compute
• Verifiable Runtime
• Verifiable Knowledge

Each addresses a different part of trust in autonomous AI.

Verifiable Compute establishes hardware-rooted evidence about AI execution.

Built around trusted execution environments, it creates cryptographic certificates for AI workflows.

@hedera’s documented role includes anchoring these attestations through its Consensus Service.

Verifiable Runtime extends oversight to agents while they operate.

Using NVIDIA BlueField DPUs and DOCA Argus, EQTY describes a separate enforcement environment for monitoring behavior, checking authorization and protecting policies from agent interference.

Verifiable Knowledge extends verification to the information agents use.

Its scope includes RAG datasets, configuration files and agent skills.

The questions become:

Where did this come from?
Which version was used?
What permissions governed access?

NVIDIA’s DOCA components have distinct roles:

• Argus observes security-relevant behavior.
• Flow governs network communications.
• Vault governs file access.

EQTY’s notary assembles the resulting signals into cryptographically linked records.

The proposed applications are interesting.

@EQTYLab describes work with Accenture on catalogs for certified agents and skills.

It also identifies NVIDIA Omniverse use cases: tracing synthetic training data and digital-twin outputs for audits.

The commercial vision: agents whose knowledge and usage rights remain verifiable when licensed or shared across organizations.

That could support new ways to price access and compensate contributors.

It is a product vision, not evidence of an established market.

Where does @hedera enter?

A separate official case study explicitly connects:

• EQTY’s AI Guardian
• Accenture’s multi-agent gateway
• NVIDIA DGX Cloud
• Hedera Consensus Service

The stated focus is verifiable AI oversight for the public sector.

9/ In that architecture, HCS provides timestamped, auditable records of agent activity.

EQTY supplies cryptographic evidence and governance tooling.

The underlying hardware supplies protected execution.

These components perform different, complementary functions.

@Accenture’s role goes beyond its Hedera Council membership.

The case study says it is developing implementation playbooks and pricing models to integrate the modules into public-sector ERP systems.

That is a concrete route toward customer deployment.

@ServiceNow also appears in this ecosystem.

@EQTYLab documents native connectors to ServiceNow, @PalantirTech and Databricks for integration with enterprise remediation tools.

A connector establishes interoperability. It does not establish platform-wide Hedera adoption.

The June Verifiable Knowledge article does not explicitly name Hedera.

HCS anchoring is documented for Verifiable Compute and the Accenture solution. Its precise use across the newer Knowledge features still needs confirmation.

Cryptographic provenance also has limits.

Evidence of source, integrity and authorization does not, by itself, prove that an AI answer is factually correct.

It gives reviewers a stronger basis for investigating how a result was produced.

The development worth following:

Execution evidence → runtime controls → knowledge provenance.

@hedera already has a documented role within this wider architecture.

An open-source AI pentesting agent has just become a case study in how quickly offensive AI tooling can move from research software to real-world attacks.
CrowdStrike linked ARTEX to a campaign against South Korean financial organizations that resulted in data exfiltration. The attacker used ARTEX alongside external AI models and Claude Code, with researchers finding session histories, configuration files and AI memory files on attacker-controlled infrastructure.
The developer has now converted ARTEX to closed source and stopped public releases.
The important detail is that ARTEX is not itself a frontier model. It is an agentic layer that connects models to tools and executes penetration-testing workflows.
That distinction matters. The security risk increasingly depends on what an AI system is allowed to do, how much autonomy it has, and which tools it can operate—not just which model sits underneath it.

When users switch models or agent frameworks, their accumulated context and memory shouldn't have to start over.

Walrus Memory aims to make agent memory portable and verifiable across models and workflows, with blockchain attestations that help users verify what happened to their data.

The key insight: persistent memory becomes more valuable the longer it runs.

text:
Let's talk about $JEANPHIL and $CLAUDIA, and why I'm bullish on the AI Influencer + short-form video narrative.

GTBxUiw6wJdmmkCGZgRHLyYxqu1vG4KtRpeox6yDpump 
2j5SaS7xy776qCBpyPQbZjyQSAtKiFgrwjfErthnW2ZM 

First, the broader sector.

I believe AI Influencers combined with short-form video distribution could become one of the narratives worth watching in the next Meme market cycle.

The underlying logic is simple: AI is turning character creation from a high-cost, low-frequency process into a low-cost, scalable content business that can be operated continuously. In the past, building an influencer required appearance, performance, filming, editing, and long-term management. Now, creators can use AI to design characters, develop personalities, produce short videos, and even operate multiple virtual personas simultaneously.

But what really matters isn't how many characters AI can generate. It's whether those characters can consistently produce content that people want to watch, discuss, and follow.

Short-form video drives distribution, characters accumulate attention, and Memes can become a speculative vehicle for that attention in the crypto market. An AI character can build a distinctive persona through continuous video releases, participate in trending topics, create new memes, and interact with other characters, gradually evolving from a single viral clip into a recognizable IP.

Compared with traditional Memes that rely on an isolated event or a single image, these characters theoretically have the ability to continuously generate new material for distribution. If a character develops a stable audience and cultural recognition, it no longer has to rely entirely on a single viral moment to maintain attention.

If this model gains traction in the crypto market, speculation may shift beyond the next viral image toward AI characters that have already attracted genuine attention on platforms like TikTok and Instagram, can consistently produce content, and have the potential to channel that external attention on-chain.

This is why I've chosen to take a deeper look at JEANPHIL and CLAUDIA. They represent two different paths within this emerging narrative.

JEANPHIL: External traction that has already emerged.

Jean Phil is an AI-generated French male character. His blond bowl cut, curled mustache, brown houndstooth suit, and signature street-style boxing moves create a recognizable visual identity that is easy to imitate.

The character has attracted significant attention on TikTok and Instagram, generating imitations and derivative content. This demonstrates how an AI character with a distinctive persona and a simple, replicable video format can quickly capture attention on mainstream social platforms.

The logic is straightforward: the character attracts external traffic, the content inspires imitations and remixes, and that attention may eventually flow into its on-chain token.

Compared with Memes that rely solely on narratives originating within crypto, JEANPHIL already has an external source of attention. What it needs to prove next is whether that momentum can persist and whether the character's popularity can translate into sustained token demand.

CLAUDIA: From AI creation toward long-term IP development.

CLAUDIA is more focused on long-term IP development. Around Claudia, anabology has been building Claudia Gallery and proposed creating an open version of Hatsune Miku for the AI era. Related initiatives also include AI character creation tools, Agent Skills, and Claudia Local.

The Influencer mode brings this vision closer to the AI Influencer model: by continuously producing videos, maintaining a consistent character identity, and experimenting with high-frequency publishing, it aims to gradually build its own audience.

The logic is that AI lowers content production costs, continuous video output helps establish character recognition, and the character gradually accumulates an audience before attempting to convert that external attention into IP influence and on-chain interest.

Compared with JEANPHIL, CLAUDIA has greater potential in the direction of a long-term AI creator ecosystem. The goal isn't simply to make a character go viral in the short term, but to explore how an AI character can continuously produce content, build an audience, and develop into an expandable, open IP.

However, this path has a longer chain of validation. Being able to produce videos consistently doesn't mean the content will necessarily gain traction. Having creation tools doesn't guarantee the ability to build a successful character. And an open-IP vision doesn't automatically mean the token can capture the resulting value.

Although both projects fall under the broader AI Influencer narrative, their trading theses are different.

JEANPHIL is more focused on existing external traction. The key question is whether that attention can persist and translate into token demand. CLAUDIA is more focused on AI creation capabilities and long-term IP development. The key question is whether it can consistently produce compelling content and build a genuine audience.

What I'm bullish on is the shared potential behind both approaches: AI characters could evolve beyond static images into dynamic IPs that continuously produce content, participate in trending topics, build social relationships, and generate new Memes.

Of course, a compelling sector narrative doesn't mean every related token will appreciate.

We need to distinguish three separate outcomes: an AI character gaining attention, an IP building lasting influence, and a token capturing value from that influence. A character can become popular without benefiting its token. A project can have impressive creation tools without producing viral content. Even if an IP continues to grow, attention may remain entirely off-chain if the token has no meaningful connection to its development.

Therefore, what I'm really looking for isn't the first token to announce that it uses AI, but projects that have demonstrated their ability to attract external attention, consistently produce distributable content, and establish a clear connection between that attention and their tokens.

AI is the production tool, short-form video is the distribution channel, character IP is the vehicle for attention, and the token represents a separate speculative market.

When these four elements become genuinely connected, AI Influencers could evolve from a trending concept into a new Meme narrative with sustained distribution potential.

In my view, the projects most likely to break out will need a distinctive character identity, consistent content distribution, a genuine external audience, and a mechanism for translating attention into token demand. That's why I'm bullish on this direction and have chosen to take a deeper look at JEANPHIL and CLAUDIA.

text:
Goldman is now projecting that Samsung HBM revenue could go from roughly $20 billion in 2026 to $74 billion in 2027.

That is a MASSIVE 274% increase in just one year.

And Samsung doesn't necessarily need HBM shipments to grow anywhere near that fast to achieve those numbers. As AI companies continue demanding more high bandwidth memory, suppliers are gaining significantly more pricing power. HBM pricing could potentially increase from around $1.50 to $3.60 per gigabit. That is an enormous increase, and when you combine higher prices with growing shipment volumes, you can see why Goldman is projecting such ridiculous revenue growth.

And remember, higher memory prices don't just increase revenue. They can also lead to MUCH higher profit margins because the cost of producing additional memory doesn't necessarily rise at the same rate as selling prices. Samsung also has enormous exposure to conventional DRAM and NAND, where stronger pricing could provide additional earnings upside. Goldman expects HBM to account for roughly 19% of Samsung's DRAM revenue in 2027, which shows how quickly this business could become a much bigger contributor.

This is exactly why I continue to believe Samsung is one of the most underrated AI memory stocks in the market. If Samsung can execute on HBM4, capture additional market share, and benefit from these higher memory prices, I believe its earnings over the next few years could surprise a LOT of investors.
